title: C++ Study Tracker
description: A 26-week plan for learning C++ (C++20) from a Python background: LearnCpp.com, then A Tour of C++ (3rd ed.), then Effective Modern C++, with problem practice and projects.

weeks.goal: Get a working C++ toolchain and write your first programs
weeks.why: Unlike Python, C++ is compiled before it runs. Setting up warnings and the C++20 standard now means the compiler catches mistakes for you for the rest of the course. Skim 0.1–0.3 and the Python-familiar parts of Ch 1; slow down on 1.6 (undefined behaviour).

weeks.goal: Split programs across files, and learn to debug
weeks.why: Headers and multi-file builds are how every real C++ project is organised. A debugger plus sanitizers will save you more time than any other skill. Ch 3 is short but high-value, so don't skip it.

weeks.goal: Understand C++'s fixed-size types and their limits
weeks.why: Python integers never overflow and there's one string type. In C++, ints have fixed sizes, overflow is undefined behaviour, and there are two string types. This is the biggest early mindset shift, and overflow comes up in interviews.

weeks.goal: Learn operator pitfalls and how names and lifetimes work
weeks.why: Operators look like Python's but hide traps: integer division, side effects, float comparison. Ch 7 explains scope, linkage and duration: where a name is visible and how long an object lives. Ch O (bit manipulation) is optional; come back to it before interviews.

weeks.goal: Control flow, random numbers, and handling bad input
weeks.why: Loops and branches are familiar from Python, so move quickly through 8.1–8.12. The new skills are random numbers and validating std::cin input. Problem practice starts this week.

weeks.goal: Type conversions and your first templates
weeks.why: C++ converts types silently in ways that cause real bugs; list initialisation and auto help you avoid them. Function templates are C++'s compile-time answer to Python's duck typing.

weeks.goal: References and pointers, part 1
weeks.why: This is the core of C++ and the most common source of interview questions. Python hides it all behind object references. Go slowly, draw memory diagrams, and type out every example.

weeks.goal: Finish pointers, then define your own types
weeks.why: In/out parameters and std::optional complete the pointers chapter. Enums and structs are your first user-defined types and the stepping stone to classes next week.

weeks.goal: Classes: bundling data with behaviour
weeks.why: Classes let you enforce invariants, rules an object always keeps true. Python has classes too, but C++ adds access control, const member functions and constructors that matter for correctness.

weeks.goal: Destructors and std::vector
weeks.why: Destructors are the first half of RAII, C++'s core idea for managing resources. std::vector is the container you'll use most, in projects and in nearly every interview problem.

weeks.goal: Fixed-size arrays and C-style arrays
weeks.why: std::array is the modern choice, but C-style arrays, decay and pointer arithmetic show up in older code and interviews. This week completes the memory-and-classes foundation before you start building.

weeks.goal: Algorithms and manual heap memory
weeks.why: Using new and delete by hand shows you exactly what smart pointers and containers protect you from. Saturday becomes build day, starting with your own Vector<T>.

weeks.goal: Stack vs heap, recursion and lambdas
weeks.why: Knowing where objects live explains lifetimes. Lambdas make the <algorithm> library, and many LeetCode solutions, short and readable.

weeks.goal: Consolidation week
weeks.readings: Revisit Ch 12 and 19; LearnCpp Appendix B
weeks.why: Good courses leave a buffer before the hardest material. Revisit what didn't stick, get an overview of modern C++, and finish Vector<T> so it passes the checkpoint.

weeks.goal: Operator overloading
weeks.why: Overloading lets your types behave like built-ins (+, ==, <<, []). It also sets up next week's key topic: copying objects correctly.

weeks.goal: Copying correctly, then rvalue references
weeks.why: Shallow vs. deep copying is where manual memory management goes wrong. Rvalue references open the door to move semantics, the defining feature of modern C++.

weeks.goal: Move semantics and smart pointers
weeks.why: This is how modern C++ manages ownership without leaks, and one of the most-asked C++ interview topics. Add a move constructor to your Vector<T> to see it working.

weeks.goal: Object relationships and inheritance basics
weeks.why: Composition vs. inheritance is a core design decision. Most good C++ prefers composition, and being able to say why is a design-interview talking point.

weeks.goal: Inheritance in depth, then polymorphism
weeks.why: Overriding behaviour in derived classes leads straight to virtual functions, which let one interface run different code at runtime.

weeks.goal: Virtual functions and the vtable
weeks.why: How virtual dispatch works under the hood (vtables, slicing, virtual destructors) is a classic C++ interview question. Aim to explain it on a whiteboard.

weeks.goal: Class templates and exceptions
weeks.why: Templates let you write generic containers like Vector<T> properly. Exceptions are how C++ reports errors, and why destructors must clean up during stack unwinding.

weeks.goal: Finish exceptions and I/O, and complete LearnCpp
weeks.why: noexcept ties back to move semantics, and file I/O is what your projects need for saving data. Finishing LearnCpp completes the core course.

weeks.goal: A Tour of C++, part 1: the language as a whole
weeks.readings: A Tour of C++ (3rd ed.) Ch 1–8
weeks.why: A fast second pass, written by C++'s creator, ties together everything you've learned and shows the modern way to write it.

weeks.goal: A Tour of C++, part 2: the standard library
weeks.readings: A Tour of C++ (3rd ed.) Ch 9–19
weeks.why: Interview solutions and real projects lean on the standard library. Know what's available: containers, algorithms, ranges and utilities.

weeks.goal: Effective Modern C++: type deduction and modern habits
weeks.why: Each item fixes one specific pitfall. Read an item, then test its examples on Compiler Explorer. Items 14–17 are worth reading later.

weeks.goal: Effective Modern C++: smart pointers and move semantics
weeks.why: These items deepen the two most interview-relevant topics of the course. Carry on with the remaining items after week 26.
